vulns.description: `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.  Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.  Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A `SoftFileLease` waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration`. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.  Classification from the review: security, conditional, by mechanism. It is the same cross-UID primitive (a UID is a user account's numeric id) as the stale-break inode-reuse race reported in a separate advisory: an inode number reused after the other user's unlink in a sticky directory, which our review reproduced across UIDs, plus a forged future mtime. The scanner rated it high (CWE-694) and demonstrated it across UIDs in its own runs. It did not fire in 250 attempts of ours over ext4 with inode reuse confirmed, nor in the scanner-side triage, so its cross-user claim rests on the report's own runs and on the mechanism.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. In the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock. - The directory is on a filesystem that reuses a freed inode number at once: ext4, and overlayfs on it (thousands of create/unlink cycles returned one number). tmpfs does not reuse one, so the pair cannot repeat there; btrfs does not either. - File timestamps come from a coarse clock whose future values the other user can compute (`CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE`, 4 ms steps on Linux 6.1; 20,000 file creations all carried that clock's value). - At least two processes of the lock user are waiting on the lock while the other user's file is there. The other user does not choose which processes overlap or when; each attempt blocks the lock for 2.2 s (for a lease, `lease_duration`). - No symbolic link, hard link or FIFO takes part, so the `fs.protected_*` sysctls (Linux settings that restrict following links and opening pipes in sticky world-writable directories) play no part. `StrictSoftFileLock` keys its watch the same way but only raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`, so it breaks no lock there.  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the watch is [`SoftFileLock._marker_unchanged_for`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L125-L132), with its caller in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123). The [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) paths hand an unparsable marker to the same code. The re-check in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118) compares the values the contender just read.  ## Introduced  0f7c4d3794dc ("fix(soft): expire leases on the contender's clock", #796, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Earlier releases compared the marker's mtime with the wall clock, and this does not affect them.  ## Mechanism  `SoftFileLock._acquire` creates the marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` (create the file, fail if it exists) and only then writes the holder record. In between it calls `fstat` and `uname`, stats `/proc/self/ns/pid` and reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, so for about 75 µs (measured) the marker exists and is empty. A contender that polls in that gap must not take the marker for garbage, and the check that protects it is the two-second watch. `_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker, finds no holder, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)` only if `_marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino)` reaches `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2.0 s). That function keeps `self._marker_seen = ((mtime, ino), first seen)` across polls and returns the elapsed monotonic time (time from a clock that only moves forward) while the pair repeats.  Neither half of the pair belongs to one file. A file's owner sets its mtime to any value with `utime`, a future time included, and ext4 gives the inode number of an unlinked file to the next file created in the directory.  1. While the lock is free, the other user creates an empty file at the lock path (inode `I`) and sets its mtime to `T`, a tick of the coarse clock about 2.2 s in the future. 2. Every waiting process of the lock user polls each 50 ms, reads an empty file and records `_marker_seen = ((T, I), first seen)`. After 2 s each poll calls `break_lock_file`, whose `rename` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted; seen with `strace`): the directory is sticky and the file belongs to the other user. `suppress(OSError, ...)` swallows the error, the file stays, and nothing resets `_marker_seen`. 3. When the coarse clock reaches `T`, the other user unlinks its file. Inode `I` is free. 4. Process F of the lock user polls during tick `T`. Its `O_EXCL` create succeeds, and its marker is inode `I` with mtime `T`. 5. Process S polls before F has written its record. It reads an empty file with pair `(T, I)`, `_marker_unchanged_for` returns the 2.2 s that S spent watching the other user's file, and S calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, T, I)`. 6. `break_lock_file` compares mtime and inode before and after its rename, but with the values S just read from F's marker, so both checks pass. F's marker has S's UID, so the rename and the unlink succeed. 7. F writes its record into the unlinked inode and returns from `acquire()`. The path is empty, so the next contender to poll creates a marker and returns from `acquire()` too. F's release finds another inode at the path (`_unlink_open_marker`) and leaves it. Neither holder learns anything.  Step 4 needs a poll inside one 4 ms tick, and step 5 a second poll inside F's 75 µs gap. Step 5 is far likelier than independent 50 ms timers would make it, because contenders that wait together bunch. With filelock's DEBUG messages timestamped, nine waiters polled within 2 to 3 ms of one another, several 0.1 ms apart or closer. In a run where the other user also recorded what replaced its file, 13 of 100 successors appeared in tick `T`, and a waiter broke 7 of those 13.  `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` hand an unparsable marker to the same code, and the lease uses the clock a second time, for expiry: `if owner.mode == "lease" and self._marker_unchanged_for(mtime, ino) >= self._lease_duration: break_lock_file(...)`. `_marker_seen` is one attribute, so the same empty file primes this branch, and step 5 has no gap to hit. To every waiter, F's complete lease record with pair `(T, I)` has gone unrefreshed for `lease_duration`, until F's first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs). With the lock user's processes using `SoftFileLease(path, lease_duration=2)` and holding for 1 s, the same other user produced an overlap in 17 of 30 attempts. The superseded holder's `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) reported `owner-changed` 0.67 s after it had entered, at its first heartbeat; a holder that releases before that is not told at all.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.  **`repro`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import shutil import subprocess import sys import time  LOCK_DIR = "/tmp/locks" LOCK_PATH = "/tmp/locks/app.lock" HOLDS_LOG = "/tmp/holds.log"   def start_victims():     # a root-owned sticky directory like /tmp, and ten processes of user victim taking turns on one lock in it     shutil.rmtree(LOCK_DIR, ignore_errors=True)     os.mkdir(LOCK_DIR)     os.chmod(LOCK_DIR, 0o1777)     victim = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim.py", LOCK_PATH]     with open(HOLDS_LOG, "w") as holds_log:         return [             subprocess.Popen(victim, stdout=holds_log, user="victim", group="victim", extra_groups=[])             for _ in range(10)         ]   def holds_entered_after(moment):     holds = []     for line in open(HOLDS_LOG):         fields = dict(field.split("=") for field in line.split())         hold = {"entered": float(fields["entered"]), "exited": float(fields["exited"]), "line": line.strip()}         if hold["entered"] > moment:             holds.append(hold)     return sorted(holds, key=lambda hold: hold["entered"])   def attack_until_overlap(phase, date_offset_s, max_attempts):     victims = start_victims()     attacker = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker.py", LOCK_PATH, str(date_offset_s)]     for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):         run = subprocess.run(attacker, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, check=True,                              user="attacker", group="attacker", extra_groups=[])         print(f"{phase} attempt {attempt}: {run.stdout.strip()}", flush=True)         unlinked_at = float(run.stdout.split("unlinked_at=")[1])         time.sleep(0.4)  # a hold lasts 0.3 s: whoever entered after the unlink has logged it by now          # A hold entered within 1 ms of the unlink can also come from a separate flaw in break_lock_file (see the         # report), so those are left out. time.monotonic() is one clock for every process on the machine.         holds = holds_entered_after(unlinked_at + 0.001)         overlaps = [(first, second) for first, second in zip(holds, holds[1:])                     if second["entered"] < first["exited"]]         if overlaps:             break     for victim in victims:         victim.kill()         victim.wait()     return overlaps   # control: the attacker's file is dated an hour after the tick in which it is unlinked control = attack_until_overlap("CONTROL", date_offset_s=3600, max_attempts=20) # attack: the same file dated at that tick, i.e. with the mtime a victim's marker created in that tick gets observed = attack_until_overlap("OBSERVED", date_offset_s=0, max_attempts=250)  # check: no two victims may ever be inside the lock at once for phase, overlaps in [("CONTROL", control), ("OBSERVED", observed)]:     print(f"{phase}: {len(overlaps)} time(s) two victims inside the lock at once")     for first, second in overlaps:         print(f"{phase}:   {first['line']}")         print(f"{phase}:   {second['line']}") print("BUG" if observed and not control else "OK") ```  **`repro.d/attacker.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import random import sys import time  lock_path, date_offset_s = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])  CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE = 5  # <linux/time.h>; the kernel stamps new files from it, and it moves once per timer tick tick_ns = round(time.clock_getres(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) * 1e9)  # take the lock path the moment it is free, like any contender while True:     try:         fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)         break     except FileExistsError:         time.sleep(0.002)  # Left empty for longer than the 2 s filelock gives an unparsable marker. The victims poll every 50 ms: the random # part makes some attempts free the path just before one of their polls. park_s = random.uniform(2.2, 2.25) release_tick = time.clock_gettime_ns(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) + round(park_s * 1e9 / tick_ns) * tick_ns mtime_ns = release_tick + date_offset_s * 10**9 os.utime(fd, ns=(mtime_ns, mtime_ns)) inode = os.fstat(fd).st_ino os.close(fd)  time.sleep(park_s - 0.05) while time.clock_gettime_ns(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) < release_tick:     pass os.unlink(lock_path)  # a marker created before the next tick gets mtime == release_tick and, on ext4, this inode unlinked_at = time.monotonic() time.sleep(0.1)  # exiting right away keeps a CPU busy during the victims' polls, and overlaps get much rarer print(f"inode={inode} mtime_ns={mtime_ns} unlinked_in_tick={release_tick} unlinked_at={unlinked_at}") ```  **`repro.d/victim.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import sys import time  from filelock import SoftFileLock  lock = SoftFileLock(sys.argv[1]) while True:     with lock:         entered = time.monotonic()         time.sleep(0.3)  # work on whatever the lock protects         print(f"pid={os.getpid()} entered={entered} exited={time.monotonic()} is_locked={lock.is_locked}", flush=True)     time.sleep(0.05) ```  ## Attack sequence  ```mermaid sequenceDiagram     participant X as other local user     participant P as lock path (sticky dir, ext4, 4 ms clock ticks)     participant S as process S of the lock user (waiting)     participant F as process F of the lock user     X->>P: create empty file, inode I, utime to future tick T     S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I), watch starts     Note over S: after 2 s each poll calls break_lock_file, rename gets EPERM, error swallowed, watch keeps counting     rect rgb(255, 214, 214)         X->>P: at tick T: unlink own file, I is free         F->>P: O_EXCL create in tick T: inode I, mtime T, record not yet written         S->>P: poll: empty file, key (T, I) seen for 2.2 s: break_lock_file(T, I) renames and unlinks F's marker         F->>P: writes record into the unlinked inode, acquire() returns         Note over S,F: the path is empty, the next contender creates a marker: two holders, no error     end ```  ## Evidence  The scanner's reproducer runs ten copies of a default-option `SoftFileLock` program (0.3 s of work per hold, 50 ms between holds) as user `victim` in a root-owned `1777` directory on overlayfs over ext4 (Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14). A program running as user `attacker` waits until the lock path is free, creates an empty file there, dates it to a coarse-clock tick 2.2 to 2.25 s ahead, and unlinks it when `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` reaches that tick. Control attempts date the file an hour after the unlink tick (20 attempts, 0 overlaps); the other attempts date it at that tick.  In four runs the overlap came after 9, 12, 27 and 20 attempts. Each showed the hold lines of two `victim` processes overlapping in time with `is_locked=True`, for example `pid=217 entered=241.295272609 exited=241.59542327` and `pid=216 entered=241.295518489 exited=241.595641553`. 40 of 650 attempts over seven runs ended this way, none with the file dated 4 ms earlier (100 attempts) or an hour later (150). A stepped run (one process stalled 0.2 s between creating its marker and writing its record, one waiting contender) deleted the fresh marker in 3 of 3 trials with the matching date and 0 of 5 with other dates.  Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` (the host's btrfs does not hand a freed number back) with inode reuse confirmed (inode 18 reused on every attempt, `--cpus 2`). 0 of 250 attempts fired on 4.2.0 in 802 s, as in the scanner-side triage, and 0 of 250 on the head of #843, so our run gives no evidence either way. The review confirmed that `utime` cannot set the file's change time. The classification follows from the cross-UID inode-reuse primitive verified in the stale-break race of the separate advisory and from the report's own runs.  ## Impact  A local user who can create a file in a soft lock's directory, a sticky directory such as `/tmp` included, gets two processes of another user to hold the same `SoftFileLock` at once (`MarkerSoftFileLock` too, by the shared code). Neither process learns of the overlap, so both modify the data the lock protects. The other user has no simpler way to get this: in the sticky directory its `unlink`, `rename`, `open(..., "w")` and `utime` on a marker of the lock user all fail, and deleting its own file only frees the lock. For `SoftFileLease` the effect is a live, refreshed claim taken after milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration` without a refresh. The holder learns of it one heartbeat later, or not at all if it releases first. Not affected: releases before 4.1.0, filesystems that do not reuse inode numbers at once (tmpfs, btrfs), and a lock with a single contender.  ## Workarounds  Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or put the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. Raise `poll_interval` so fewer waiters bunch inside one clock tick; this lowers the hit rate but does not close the window.  ## Patched version  4.2.1.  Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/843  ## Credits  Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner (automated analysis), 15 October 2026; reviewed by the maintainers.  - 2026-10-15 23:08 UTC: report received (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`, scanned commit b831496b0273) - 2026-10-16 00:46 UTC: draft advisory created - 2026-10-16 01:42 UTC: fix PR #843 opened

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The process writes bytes of the other user's choosing from offset 0 into any non-empty regular file the lock user can write, resized to a whole number of pages, provided the other user can create `<file>-journal` beside it (the lock user's own `0600` files in `/tmp` qualify). Without a journal the process creates an empty file at any path it may create, or converts a WAL-mode SQLite database of its own to rollback mode with no error. A journal beside a swapped-in database makes the process unlink one regular file of the other user's choosing per journal; the acquire succeeds and raises nothing. A process inside `write_lock()` stops excluding the lock user's other processes from `read_lock()`, and the holder can die from a `SIGBUS` that arrives in `release()`.  It is **not** reachable for a database the lock user owns in `/tmp` with `fs.protected_regular` 1 or 2. There only the planted `-wal` denial of service remains: every acquire raises an undocumented `sqlite3.OperationalError` that `Timeout` and `OSError` handlers do not catch. It is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (4.0.9), which refused the symlink at the database path but followed it at `<database> (deleted)`. Windows does not take this path.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. - For a lock in a sticky directory keep `fs.protected_regular` at 1 or 2 and `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (distribution defaults). Treat a sudden `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<db>-wal` beside the database that the file's owner or root has to remove.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. The other user plays both the stale holder and the "successor" the branch exists for:  1. The other user leaves a genuine marker of a dead process at the lock path (a forked child takes the lock and `_exit`s). The lock user's `_try_break_stale_lock()` reads it and `owner_is_stale()` agrees, so `break_lock_file()` renames it to `app.lock.break.<pid>.<token>`. In a directory without the sticky bit the lock user may rename a file it does not own. 2. The other user still owns that file and gives it a newer mtime (modification time) after the `lstat` on line 113. Line 117 then takes it for a recreated marker, and line 119 sees a regular file. 3. The other user renames a symbolic link to the lock user's private file over the break name. 4. Line 121 resolves the link with the lock user's credentials, so `app.lock` becomes a second hard link to the private file. Line 122 removes the symbolic link.  The other user's own `os.link()` on the private file fails with `EACCES` (it cannot enter the `0700` directory). On a file of the lock user it can reach, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` answers `EPERM` (operation not permitted). The lock user would evict the odd "marker" after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2 s), so the other user moves it to another name first, which the non-sticky directory allows. Both steps are races against a few lines of Python. There are about 40 µs between the `lstat` on line 113 and the one on line 117 (half of it the `rename`), and about 2 µs between line 117 and the `os.link()` call. inotify tells the other user when to act. A watch reports the lock user closing the marker after reading it, then the rename together with the break name. Evidence  The scanner's reproducer takes about 5 s and is deterministic. Root creates `/home/victim/private` (`0700`) with `signing.key` (17 bytes, `0600`) and `/tmp/shared-locks` (`0777`, no sticky bit), with `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1` and `fs.protected_symlinks = 1`. Then the `attacker` child leaves `app.lock held by pid 253 which has exited`. The `victim` account runs `with SoftFileLock(path)` under `strace -P ... -e inject=rename:delay_exit=2000000 -e inject=linkat:delay_enter=2000000`, which holds it 2 s after its `rename()` and 2 s before its `linkat()` without changing any call. The `attacker` account bumps the break file, swaps in the symbolic link, and renames `app.lock` to `other.lock`.  The result line reads `signing.key: links=2, names in /tmp/shared-locks with its inode: ['other.lock']`, and after the `victim` account's second program takes `FileLock('/tmp/shared-locks/other.lock')`, `size=0`. The unpaused variant (`unpaused_victim.py` looping on the lock, `unpaused_attacker.py` timing both steps with inotify) won 10 runs out of 10 on the 2-CPU image after 9 to 910 lock cycles (1 to 65 s); one run won after 128 cycles (8 s). On macOS 27.0.1 (CPython 3.13.16) a plain `os.link` of a symbolic link follows it (target `st_nlink` 2) while `follow_symlinks=False` links the symbolic link itself, which confirms the report's macOS note.  ## Impact  A local user who can write a lock directory that has no sticky bit makes a user of a soft lock in that directory create a hard link there to one of that user's own files on the same filesystem, including files inside directories the other user cannot enter. The content stays unreadable, but the other user now reads size, times, mode and owner of the file through the new name, keeps the inode alive after the lock user deletes or rotates the file, and holds what `fs.protected_hardlinks` exists to deny, a name it can move around for someone else's file.  Whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on the file, and filelock 4.2.0 was such a consumer itself. `UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd()` ran `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)` on whatever regular file `O_NOFOLLOW` let it open. The other user moved the link to `other.lock`, the lock user took `FileLock("other.lock")`, and the 17-byte private file became 0 bytes. The other user can also move the link into sticky `/tmp` on the same filesystem before the lock user locks it there, and a `FileLock` with a permissive `mode` such as `0o666` applied that mode to the private file too, after which the other user could write its content.  On its own, without such a second lock, the result is the link and the metadata above. The other user has to win two short races and needs the lock user to take the lock more than once. Not affected: sticky directories on the tested settings, CPython 3.11 on Linux, releases before 4.1.0.  ## Workarounds  Keep soft locks out of directories other users can write without the sticky bit; a `0700` directory of the lock's user, or a sticky directory, is not affected. On CPython 3.11 on Linux the swap has no effect. Do not take a native `FileLock` on a name another user controls.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.  With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.  The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private `.filelock-*` link directories with `shutil.rmtree` (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.  Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO` [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L` scores 6.1 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): two `rename` calls and no race against filelock's own code. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user destroys a directory tree owned by the lock user, and the lock user's program reports no error. `A:L` (partial availability loss): the Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant makes the lock user's first lock construction fail. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges. That is a `0777` directory, or a group-writable one (in a setgid `2775` directory a group member can rename the lock user's sub-directory the same way). Renaming an entry needs write permission on the parent only, not on the entry. Anyone who can write the parent can rename a `0700` directory of the lock user. - Sticky directories (`/tmp` itself, any `1777` directory) stop the release variant: the rename of an entry owned by the lock user fails with `EPERM`. The dead-owner sweep still reaches a lock user's tree that sits inside a directory the other account owns there. That account may rename its own directory to a forged dead-owner name, and the lock user's sweep deletes everything inside it. The Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant also works in a sticky directory. - Platform and route. The lock user must connect through the private hard link. That is every `ReadWriteLock` or `AsyncReadWriteLock` on macOS (since 4.1.1, #820), or a POSIX process whose `/proc/self/fd/<n>` (`/dev/fd/<n>` elsewhere) does not exist, such as a chroot or container without `/proc`. Linux with `/proc` mounted connects through the descriptor and creates no `.filelock-*` directory (checked: none appears, also with two holders in one process), so stock Linux is not affected at 4.2.0. The reproducer runs the same Python code on Linux with `/proc` hidden, which takes root and is test scaffolding, not a step the other user performs. Windows does not take this route. - Target set. Only directories that sit in the shared parent itself, or that the other account can already write, are reachable. The kernel refuses to move a `0700` directory of the lock user in from another parent. A lock user running as root deletes a tree of any owner. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. Nothing ties that path to the directory filelock created. `mkdtemp` makes the name unpredictable and the directory `0700`. The name is in the parent's listing as soon as it exists (`ls -a`), and renaming it needs write permission on the parent only. `0700` keeps the other user out of the directory; it does not stop a rename of the directory. There are two ways in, with the same preconditions.  **On release.** A connection lives for one acquisition: `_open_for_acquisition` opens it and `release()` reaches `close` through `_release` and `_finish_connection`. The code trusts the path from the acquire to the release, for as long as the application keeps the lock. While the lock user holds `write_lock()` on `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db`, the directory lists `.filelock-<pid>--<host digest>-<random>/` (`0700`, owned by the lock user, containing `lock.db`). The first connect of every process on the link route runs it, the validation connection included. It runs `rmtree` on every `.filelock-*` directory whose name parses as a dead owner's. It checks neither the directory's owner, nor its mode, nor whether it holds only `lock.db`. `_owner_is_gone` splits the name after `.filelock-` into `pid`, `start`, `digest` (a hash of the host name) and a suffix. Without filelock that user can rename such a directory but cannot remove a non-empty one whose contents they have no permission on. With filelock the lock user's process destroys the contents. The release variant needs two `rename` calls at any point while the lock user holds the lock and wins no race against filelock's own code. The sweep variant needs one rename and no held lock, and fires on the next lock construction by any lock user process in that directory. The real link directory stays under its new name with an extra hard link to the database.  It is **not** reachable on stock Linux with `/proc` mounted at 4.2.0. The release variant is **not** reachable in a sticky directory. This is the same position as in GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (a user who can change names in a shared lock directory). Here the name is the derived `.filelock-*` directory rather than the database, and the redirected operation is a recursive delete.  ## Workarounds  - On macOS, and on any POSIX system where `/proc/self/fd` is unavailable, keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. - Do not keep other directories of value beside a lock database in a directory other accounts can write; the deletion targets are siblings of the database. - On Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.2.0 does not take the link route and needs no workaround for this finding.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.  Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover. - Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete. - Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails. - Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time. - What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits. - Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.  ## Mechanism  Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.  ## Reproduction  The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. `SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) refreshes its holder record (the file under `<path>.rw/holders/` that says a process holds or wants the lock) on every poll of a waiting acquire and on every heartbeat (the periodic refresh a holder runs to keep its record fresh). It does so by reopening `<path>.rw/holders/<token>` by name with a plain blocking `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` open and writing at offset 0, without checking what it opened. `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail only when the final name is a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path).  A different local user (the other user below) who owns the lock's `.rw` tree reads the token of the user running the lock (the lock user below) from the `holders/` listing and renames another node over the record. The other user owns the tree because it created it first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), or because it can write a lock directory without the sticky bit.  A FIFO (a named pipe: a file whose open for writing blocks until some process opens it for reading) makes the lock user's `write_lock()` / `read_lock()` hang regardless of `timeout`. It also stops a lock holder's heartbeat thread without `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) ever running, so the lock grants a second process while the first still believes it holds it. This works on a default Linux.  Where the kernel lets a user hard-link a file it does not own (a hard link is a second name for the same file; Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`; macOS and the BSDs by their defaults, not executed), a hard link makes the lock user overwrite the first ~135 bytes of one of its own private files with its holder record. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.0.0 and <= 4.2.0. The bytes are filelock's record, not chosen by the other user, so the change stays within that record. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes a lock user's acquire outlast any `timeout` and leaves a holder's heartbeat thread asleep. The owner of a planted `.rw` tree can make the refresh open a FIFO and stall a lock user, including its heartbeat. In sticky `/tmp`, the user who creates `/tmp/app.lock.rw/{gen,holders}` before the lock's first use owns `holders/` and may rename over anything the lock user creates in it. In a shared directory without the sticky bit, being first is not needed. 2. The lock user publishes its record and drops the descriptor. `Participant.publish()` calls `OsFiles.create()`, which opens `holders/<token>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, writes the record and closes. The token is the file name, so the other user reads it from a listing of its own directory. 3. The other user swaps the name. Hard link: `link("/home/victim/accounts.csv", "holders/link")`, then `rename("holders/link", "holders/<token>")`; `link(2)` needs search permission on `/home/victim` and write permission on `holders/`, nothing on the file. Each poll of a waiting acquire (`poll_interval`, 0.25 s) runs `advance()` → `_keep_claim_fresh()` → `_refresh_nonce()` → `overwrite()`. On `Timeout` or release, `leave()` unlinks `holders/<token>`, which is now the other user's link. The target is back to one link and `holders/` is empty. The other user makes a lock user's `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` / `read_lock` / `write_lock` hang whatever `timeout` the caller passed. That user could already keep the lock busy, in which case the lock user gets `Timeout` on time; the FIFO takes that away. Against a process that holds the lock, the FIFO stops the heartbeat thread, which is the only path by which a holder learns of its eviction. After `stale_threshold` (90 s by default) a second process takes the lock and nothing tells the first, so a live holder and its evictor both believe they hold the write lock and `on_compromise` does not run.  A user who owns the tree can already get a reader granted beside a live writer by writing one forged `gen/<N+1>` snapshot. What this bug adds is the acquire that outlasts its `timeout` and the heartbeat thread that does not return. The FIFO variant touches nothing outside the lock's own directory.  Where the kernel allows the hard link, a different local user corrupts files it has no access to, with the rights of the process that takes the lock. filelock's holder record replaces the first 135 bytes or so of the target. The other user does not choose the bytes, so the result is data destruction, not code execution: the header of a database or archive, the first lines of a configuration or credential file. This is the hard-link counterpart, on a derived name of the soft read-write lock, of the symbolic link fixes at the lock path recorded in the changelog (3.20.1 for lock file creation, 3.20.3 for `SoftFileLock`), which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. - In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can, and refuse to use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account. - Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream Linux distributions). It removes the file-overwrite variant, not the FIFO stall.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.  `O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:   - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);   - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;   - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs. - What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.  Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. Those matter for a descriptor the lock user still holds, for a second name of the file, and for programs that trust the file's ownership. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. Mutual exclusion is not affected.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the lock file in a directory no other account can write, or in a sticky directory on a filesystem where no directory holding the lock user's files is writable by others. On Linux keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream distributions), which closes the hard-link route. - Do not pass a permissive explicit `mode` (`0o666`, `0o660`, `0o644`) unless accounts share the lock; without a mode the exposure is the truncation only. - Keep the lock file in place (`preserve_lock_file=True`). Once a lock file owned by the lock user exists in a sticky directory, another user cannot rename or link over it. - Where the lock does not need `flock` semantics, `SoftFileLock` applies its mode only to the marker it created with `O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. A strict holder does not look at its claims between acquire and release, and on release `_unlink_owner_path_result` takes the `FileNotFoundError` for each missing claim as "already removed", so `_release` finishes without error. This goes beyond what holding the lock gives that user, because a held lock ends in `Timeout` when the caller's timeout runs out, and this does not. With the looping-page layout the acquiring thread spins at 100% of one CPU on a free lock, `Timeout` is not raised, Ctrl-C does not interrupt it, and only killing the process ends it. It is a denial of service of the lock user's process only: it reads nothing and corrupts nothing, and in the long-row case the lock is still granted afterwards.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. - Do not give the lock a database another account may write. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. A lock shared between accounts through a `0666` database stays reachable even in `/tmp`. - If a stall or hang appears, the file at the lock path is the cause; replacing it with an empty file restores the lock.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.  On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.22.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race, though one the other user starts, lengthens (by making the lock user's `/proc` read slow) and retries at every release. The scanner measured 10 to 26 overlaps per 20-second run. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.  Classification from the review: security, conditional on a sticky shared directory, ext4-style inode reuse and at least two contenders of the lock user. Our review verified it across UIDs (a UID is a user account's numeric id): the other user as uid 1001, the lock user's processes as uid 1000, BUG on 4.2.0 over ext4. The scanner rated it high (CWE-367).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory such as `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. The sticky bit stops it removing the lock user's marker (checked: `EPERM`, operation not permitted), so the lock user's own stale break does the deletion. - The directory is on a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file. ext4 does (six create/unlink rounds returned one number six times, in the image's overlayfs `/tmp` and on a loop-mounted ext4), and xfs does. tmpfs returned six increasing numbers and the same run there gave no overlap, and btrfs does not hand a freed number back. - The lock user has at least two processes contending for the lock, and the displaced holder is still inside when the next contender polls (the breaker itself comes back one `poll_interval`, 50 ms by default, later). - The lock is `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` (or async forms). That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. Evidence  The scanner's reproducer runs as root, drops to `victim` and `attacker` through `runuser`, needs `git`, changes no sysctl, and takes about half a second. It creates `/srv/shared` (root-owned, `0777`, no sticky bit), has `victim` run `git init /home/victim/project` and makes that directory `0700`. It then drives two programs. `victim_worker.py` holds one `SoftReadWriteLock("/srv/shared/app.lock")` with default options; for each line on stdin it takes `write_lock(timeout=30)`, releases it and prints `finished <job> and released the lock`. `attacker_swap_tree.py` renames the lock user's `app.lock.rw` aside, creates a new one with a world-writable `holders/`, and makes `app.lock.rw/gen` a symbolic link to `/home/victim/project/.git`, using only write access to `/srv/shared`. On the scanned commit it prints:  ``` CONTROL  attacker opens HEAD for writing: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/home/victim/project/.git/HEAD' VICTIM   victim: finished job 1 and released the lock VICTIM   app.lock.rw owner uid 1000 mode 0o700 ATTACK   app.lock.rw/gen -> /home/victim/project/.git CONTROL  new worker: RuntimeError: /srv/shared/app.lock.rw/gen exists but is not a directory or is a symlink; refusing to use it CONTROL  HEAD after the new worker: 'ref: refs/heads/master
' VICTIM   victim: finished job 2 and released the lock OBSERVED HEAD: '<epoch>
filelock-rw/1
generation=2
' OBSERVED .git: [..., 'epoch', '00000000000000000001', '00000000000000000002', ...] OBSERVED git status: fatal: not a git repository BUG ```  The `CONTROL` lines show that the other account cannot reach the repository itself and that a fresh lock object refuses the planted tree. The existing check works; the code does not repeat it for a live instance. The sticky-directory variant ends the same way, with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`. There the other account creates `app.lock.rw`, `gen` and `holders` with mode `0777` in a `1777` parent before the lock user's first acquire, then renames its own `gen` aside and links it to the lock user's `.git`.  Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #842 stack head: `OK`, `HEAD` stays `ref: refs/heads/master`, `.git` keeps its original listing and `git status` answers `On branch master`. The result is the same with the stack's owner check disabled, so it does not depend on who owns the tree.  ## Impact  With the lock user's privileges, in any directory the lock user can write, the other user gets a file named `HEAD` replaced, new files `epoch`, `HEAD` and 20-digit generation names created (mode `0600`), and files deleted whose names match the protocol's patterns (32 hex digits, 20 digits, `.commit-*`). The bytes written are filelock's own records, not chosen by the other user. Replacing `HEAD` makes a git repository unusable when the other user knows its path. Renaming `<path>.rw` away is something this other user may do anyway, and `docs/how-to.rst` documents the result (a new log starts). What this finding adds is that the lock user's file operations leave the lock's directory.  This is adjacent to GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (`ReadWriteLock` following a symbolic link at its database path, fixed in 4.0.9) and the earlier symbolic link fixes (PR 461 for lock file creation, PR 465 for `SoftFileLock`, PR 565 for refreshing soft read/write lock markers). Each guards the final path component. Here the link sits at a directory component, which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. - In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can (for example at install time with mode `0700`), and do not use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account. - Prefer a fresh lock object per unit of work over a long-lived singleton when other accounts can write the lock directory. A fresh object re-runs the directory check and refuses a planted tree.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. When extracting a tar archive pip may not check symbolic links point into the extraction directory if the tarfile module doesn't implement PEP 706. Note that upgrading pip to a "fixed" version for this vulnerability doesn't fix all known vulnerabilities that are remediated by using a Python version that implements PEP 706. Note that this is a vulnerability in pip's fallback implementation of tar extraction for Python versions that don't implement PEP 706 and therefore are not secure to all vulnerabilities in the Python 'tarfile' module. If you're using a Python version that implements PEP 706 then pip doesn't use the "vulnerable" fallback code. Mitigations include upgrading to a version of pip that includes the fix, upgrading to a Python version that implements PEP 706 (Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12), applying the linked patch, or inspecting source distributions (sdists) before installation as is already a best-practice.
